questions.q: Name the four approaches to human development listed in NCERT Table 3.1 and identify the economist associated with the Capability Approach.
questions.a: The four approaches are: (1) Income Approach, (2) Welfare Approach, (3) Basic Needs Approach, (4) Capability Approach. The Capability Approach is associated with Prof. Amartya Sen. A wrong answer (e.g., naming "GDP Approach" or "Growth Approach" instead of Income Approach, or attributing Capability Approach to Mahbub ul Haq) reveals confusion between the *measurement tool* (HDI by Haq) and the *philosophical foundation* (Capability Approach by Sen), or inability to distinguish the four distinct frameworks.

questions.q: Explain why the Income Approach considers higher income as equivalent to higher human development, and give one reason why this equivalence fails in practice.
questions.a: The Income Approach assumes income reflects the level of freedom an individual enjoys — more income means more choices. This fails because income growth can be unequal (e.g., rising GDP with stagnant wages for the poor), spent on non-development goods (defence, luxury imports), or earned at the cost of health/environment (industrial pollution reducing life expectancy). A student who says "income buys everything" misses that *choices* require capabilities (health, education) which income alone cannot guarantee if public goods are absent.

questions.q: A state government increases education spending by 20% but school dropout rates among girls remain unchanged. Using the Welfare Approach and Capability Approach, explain this outcome in two sentences each.
questions.a: Welfare Approach: The government fulfilled its responsibility by maximising expenditure on education (a welfare good); people are passive recipients, so if dropouts persist, it is due to household-level factors beyond state control. Capability Approach: Spending alone does not build capabilities — if girls lack *freedom* to attend (social norms, safety, sanitation, care burden), the *capability* to be educated remains unrealised. A wrong answer that blames "corruption" or "lazy parents" under both approaches shows failure to distinguish the *theoretical logic* of each framework.

questions.q: Compare the Basic Needs Approach and Capability Approach on: (a) who defines the needs, (b) role of human agency, (c) treatment of diversity. Present as a 3-row table.
questions.a:
| Dimension | Basic Needs Approach | Capability Approach |
|-----------|---------------------|---------------------|
| Who defines needs | Experts/institutions (ILO list: health, education, food, water, sanitation, housing) | Individuals/communities — needs derive from what people *value* being and doing |
| Human agency | Passive beneficiaries; provision is top-down | Active agents; development expands *freedom to choose* |
| Treatment of diversity | Uniform list for all "defined sections" | Inherent — capabilities vary by context (disability, gender, geography) |

A student who merges the two ("both provide basic needs") misses the epistemological shift: from *externally defined minimum* to *internally valued freedom*.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "The Capability Approach is just the Basic Needs Approach with a fancy name — both want people to have health, education, and food." Use Amartya Sen's distinction between *functionings* and *capabilities*.
questions.a: The critique is invalid. Basic Needs focuses on *achieved functionings* (being nourished, literate, housed) — a checklist of outcomes. Capability Approach focuses on *capabilities* — the *real freedoms* or *opportunities* to achieve those functionings. A person may have food available (capability) but choose to fast (functioning not achieved) — Basic Needs counts this as failure; Capability respects the choice. Conversely, a girl enrolled in school (Basic Need met) but pulled out for marriage lacks the *capability* to be educated. Sen's distinction: functionings = "beings and doings"; capabilities = "the freedom to achieve those beings and doings."

questions.q: Design a village-level development intervention that operationalises the Capability Approach for adolescent girls. Specify: (a) the capability targeted, (b) two conversion factors addressed, (c) one indicator of success that is NOT an enrolment or attendance number.
questions.a: (a) Capability: "Being able to participate in community decision-making" (political agency). (b) Conversion factors addressed: (i) Social norms — via facilitated dialogues with parents/elders on girls' right to speak; (ii) Physical infrastructure — safe transport to panchayat meetings. (c) Success indicator: Number of girls who *submit a written proposal* to the Gram Sabha on a local issue (e.g., water tap location) — this measures *exercised agency*, not just presence. A weak answer lists "life skills training" without specifying which capability it expands or how conversion factors (caste, gender, disability) are addressed.
